newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO and Russia to sign pact on new cooperative era.
newsitem.headline: NATO and Russia to sign pact on new cooperative era.

text.p: Former Cold War foes NATO and Russia sign an accord on Tuesday which both say will allow Eastern and Western Europe to be united in peace after more than 50 years of division.

NATO leaders and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will formally adopt a pact designed to bring Moscow to the centre of efforts to create a new European security order and ease the alliance's eastwards expansion.
"It's a big step for Russia, for NATO, for Europe and for the whole world," Yeltsin told reporters when he arrived in Paris on Monday for the official signing ceremony.
"It's good for Russia, America, France, England, Germany. They all won, all Europe won. And security won -- that's the main thing," he added.

Yeltsin, who later met the ceremony's host, French President Jacques Chirac, will be joined at the ceremony (0830 GMT) at France's grandiose Elysee Palace by U.S. President Bill Clinton and other leaders of the West's military shield.

Clinton, who arrives in Paris on Tuesday, has described the deal as a "historic event" which will allow Europe to heal the wounds of the post-World War Two carve-up of the continent into communist and non-communist camps.

Czech-born U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, herself a child of a divided Europe, also said on Monday the accord, which creates a NATO-Russia Council to give Moscow a permanent voice within the alliance, was "truly historic".
"We will all be able to participate in putting a divided Europe back together," she told reporters after meeting French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

She said The Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation would play a key role in shaping the Europe of the next century, "what Europe will be in the 21st Century, the relationship of the United States to Europe and the place of Russia within Europe."

Diplomats said Albright and de Charette had a long discussion over which countries should be invited to join the alliance at a special summit in Madrid in July and found a "considerable amount of agreement on some but not all names".
Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are the favourites and are expected to receive the necessary backing of all current 16 members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

Yeltsin has won assurances the allies have no plans to place nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the soil of the new members and has been granted a special consultative mechanism, but failed to gain any say in future NATO decisions.

Based at NATO's headquarters in Brussels, the Russia-NATO Council will have a permanent secretariat and Russia will be represented by a permanent ambassador. Twice a year, it will meet at both foreign minister and defence minister level.
Clinton says alliance expansion will right the wrongs of the Yalta conference of 1945, when most of eastern Europe was allowed to come under the "zone of influence" of Josef Stalin's Soviet Union.

Moscow is most concerned by the desire of some former Soviet republics, primarily the Baltic states Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia, to join the alliance and is angered by NATO's refusal to rule out future membership for them.

The presidents of the three states appealed to alliance leaders on Monday to make a commitment that other new members be accepted later, and issued a joint declaration reaffirming their desire to join.
